parts.prompt_html: Describe fully the plane transformation represented by \(B\) when (i) \(k=1\) and (ii) \(m=k\).
parts.answer_html: (i) A stretch parallel to the y-axis, factor \(m\). (ii) An enlargement with centre the origin, factor \(k\).
parts.solution_html: The image of \((x,y)\) is \((kx,my)\). Setting \(k=1\) leaves the x-coordinate unchanged. Setting \(m=k\) multiplies both coordinates by the same positive factor. If that factor equals 1, the transformation is the identity.
parts.hint_html: Write down the image coordinates.

marking_points.criterion_html: State the stretch direction and scale factor.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \(ABC\) and prove that it is singular for every permitted pair \((k,m)\). Show an explicit determinant calculation.
parts.answer_html:
\[ABC=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2 k & k\\2 k + 2 m & 4 k - m & 2 k + 3 m\\- k + 6 m & - 2 k - 3 m & - k + 9 m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(ABC)=0\]
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}k & 0\\2 k & m\\- k & 3 m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[ABC=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2 k & k\\2 k + 2 m & 4 k - m & 2 k + 3 m\\- k + 6 m & - 2 k - 3 m & - k + 9 m\end{pmatrix}\]

In this product, row 3 is three times row 2 minus seven times row 1. For an explicit determinant computation, expansion gives

\[\det(ABC)=k(49km)-2k(7km)+k(-35km)=0\]

Therefore the square product is singular even though \(B\) is non-singular.
parts.hint_html: Look for the same linear relation between the rows of A and of ABC.

marking_points.criterion_html: Multiply the rectangular matrices in a compatible order.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \(Ap\) and \(Bp\), and show that both \(A\) and \(B\) are singular.
parts.solution_html:
\[Ap=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[Bp=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-7\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det A=4-4=0,\qquad\det B=-2+2=0\]
parts.hint_html: Multiply a row by the column, then calculate each 2×2 determinant.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all columns \(u\) and \(v\) satisfying \(Au=Ap\) and \(Bv=Bp\), respectively.
parts.solution_html: For \(u=(u_1,u_2)^{\mathsf T}\), the only distinct condition is \(u_1+2u_2=1\). Writing \(u_2=-1+s\) gives \(u_1=3-2s\). For \(v\), the condition is \(2v_1-v_2=7\). Writing \(v_1=3+t\) gives \(v_2=-1+2t\).
parts.hint_html: Each pair of equations repeats the same condition.

marking_points.criterion_html: Reduce the image conditions to one equation for each map.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: In addition, \(u-v=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(u\) and \(v\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\binom{-2s-t}{s-2t}=\binom{-7}1\]

Thus \(2s+t=7\) and \(s-2t=1\), giving \(s=3,t=1\). Substituting gives u=(−3,2)ᵀ and v=(4,1)ᵀ.
parts.hint_html: Subtract the two parameterised columns before solving.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \(AB\) and \(BA\).
parts.solution_html:
The first product has order \(2\times2\) and the second \(3\times3\). Row-by-column multiplication gives

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Check the dimensions before multiplying.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Explain why \(AB=I_2\) does not imply that \(BA=I_3\). Show that \(BA\) is singular.
parts.answer_html: The factors are not square inverses; \(BA\ne I_3\) and \(\det(BA)=0\).
parts.solution_html: The usual inverse relation is for square matrices of the same order. Here the direct calculation gives a zero last row in BA; its determinant is therefore zero, while the last row of I₃ is not zero.
parts.hint_html: Use the actual 3×3 product rather than cancelling rectangular matrices.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Without carrying out another full multiplication, show that \((BA)^2=BA\).
parts.solution_html:
Associativity allows regrouping, but not reversing the factor order:

\[(BA)(BA)=B(AB)A=B I_2 A=BA\]
parts.hint_html: Group the middle factors AB.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: State the orders of \((2A-B)C\) and \(C(2A-B)\).
parts.solution_html: Both A and B have two rows and three columns, while C has three rows and two columns. The inner dimensions agree in both products; the outer dimensions give the stated orders.
parts.hint_html: Use rows × columns for each factor.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \((2A-B)C\).
parts.solution_html:
\[2A-B=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -4 & 6\\3 & 7 & -9\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(2A-B)C=\begin{pmatrix}-11 & 22\\26 & -34\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Complete the subtraction before multiplying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Multiply by C in the stated order.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Use the distributive law to express \(BC\) in terms of \(AC\) and \((2A-B)C\). Verify your expression numerically.
parts.solution_html:
\[AC=\begin{pmatrix}-3 & 10\\10 & -10\end{pmatrix}\]
\[2AC-(2A-B)C=\begin{pmatrix}5 & -2\\-6 & 14\end{pmatrix}=BC\]
parts.hint_html: Keep C on the right of each term.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the condition on \(p,q\) for which \(AB=0\).
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}2 p - q & 0\\6 p - 3 q & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

Both non-zero expressions vanish precisely when \(2p-q=0\). The second column already gives zero.
parts.hint_html: Compute the product entry by entry.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Give one numerical example in which \(AB=0\) but neither factor is the zero matrix. Explain why it would be invalid to cancel \(A\).
parts.answer_html:
\[B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]

A has determinant zero and has no inverse.
parts.solution_html:
Take \(p=1,q=2\). Then

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

The matrices A and B both have non-zero entries. Also \(\det A=2(-3)-(-1)6=0\), so premultiplication by \(A^{-1}\) is not available.
parts.hint_html: Cancellation requires an inverse, not merely a non-zero matrix.
parts.label: b

stem_html: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\). It is given that \(AB=BA\) and \(\det B=20\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(p\) and \(q\).
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}2 p & 2 q + 12\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}2 p & 3 p + q\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]

The upper-right entries give \(2q+12=3p+q\), so \(q=3p-12\). Since \(\det B=4p=20\), \(p=5\) and \(q=3\).
parts.hint_html: Compare corresponding entries of AB and BA.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: A student claims that \(AB=BA\) is possible only when one of the matrices is a scalar multiple of \(I\). Explain why your answer disproves this claim.
parts.answer_html: Neither matrix is a scalar multiple of I, but their products in either order agree.
parts.solution_html:
A has an off-diagonal entry 3, and the resulting B also has an off-diagonal entry 3. A scalar multiple of I has both off-diagonal entries zero. Nevertheless,

\[AB=BA=\begin{pmatrix}10 & 18\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Check what a scalar multiple of the identity looks like.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain why neither factor is a scalar identity.
Use the equal products to disprove the claim.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State the order of \(X\) and rearrange the equation to make \(X\) the subject.
parts.solution_html: AX must have the same order as C and B, so X has two rows and three columns. Subtract B, then premultiply by the inverse of A. This gives \(X=A^{-1}(C-B)\).
parts.hint_html: The inverse must multiply AX from the left.

marking_points.criterion_html: Rearrange with the inverse on the correct side.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(X\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=1\]
\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[C-B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 5\\1 & 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[X=A^{-1}(C-B)=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2 & 3\\0 & 4 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Find the small inverse first.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
Both determinants are 1. The inverse formula gives the first inverse. For B, solve \(BU=I_3\) for an upper-triangular U, or use cofactors:

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

In particular, the (1,3) entry of \(B^{-1}\) is 1, not zero.
parts.hint_html: The inverse of an upper-triangular matrix is upper triangular.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(X\), making the multiplication order clear.
parts.solution_html:
\[X=A^{-1}CB^{-1}\]
\[A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & -1\\1 & 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[X=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0\\1 & 3 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]

This has order \(2\times3\), as required.
parts.hint_html: Undo A on the left and B on the right.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why \(B^{-1}CA^{-1}\) is not an alternative expression for \(X\).
parts.answer_html: The indicated products are not even dimensionally defined.
parts.solution_html: The product \(B^{-1}C\) would multiply a \(3\times3\) matrix by a \(2\times3\) matrix. Their inner dimensions, 3 and 2, do not match.
parts.hint_html: Check dimensions rather than trying the multiplication.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: By direct multiplication, show that \(A^2=3A+4I\).
parts.solution_html:
\[A^2=\begin{pmatrix}7 & 9\\6 & 10\end{pmatrix}\]
\[3A+4I=\begin{pmatrix}7 & 9\\6 & 10\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Calculate both sides; no theorem about characteristic equations is needed.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Use this identity to find \(A^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
Rearrange the identity as \(A(A-3I)=4I\). Thus \(A\bigl(\frac14(A-3I)\bigr)=I\), and

\[A^{-1}=(A-3I)/4=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{4}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Factor A from A²−3A.

marking_points.criterion_html: Rearrange as a product equal to I.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Express \(A^4\) in the form \(uA+vI\), where \(u,v\) are integers.
parts.solution_html:
\[A^4=(3A+4I)^2=9A^2+24A+16I\]
\[=9(3A+4I)+24A+16I=51A+52I\]
parts.hint_html: A commutes with I, so expand the square and substitute once more.
parts.label: c

stem_html: A linear plane transformation maps \((1,2)\) to \((4,5)\) and \((2,1)\) to \((5,4)\). Its matrix is \(M\).

parts.prompt_html: Form a matrix equation and find \(M\).
parts.solution_html:
Put the input and output columns in matching order:

\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\5 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\5 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3}\\\dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Place the two given input vectors as columns, not rows.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the input matrix inverse on the right.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the image of \((3,-1)\). Check it by expressing the input as a linear combination of the two given inputs.
parts.solution_html:
\[M\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\binom{3}{-1}=-\frac53\binom12+\frac73\binom21\]
\[-\frac53\binom45+\frac73\binom54=\binom51\]
parts.hint_html: Use the same coefficients on the image vectors.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the area of the image of a triangle of area 7.
parts.solution_html: Since \(\det M=4-1=3\), the area is \(7|3|=21\).
parts.hint_html: Multiply by the absolute determinant.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \(AB\) and \(A^{-1}B^{-1}\), and use a product to show that the student is wrong.
parts.solution_html:
\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[A^{-1}B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})=\begin{pmatrix}7 & -2\\4 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

This last product is not I, so the proposed inverse fails.
parts.hint_html: A claimed inverse must produce I when multiplied by AB.

marking_points.criterion_html: Show a non-identity product and reject the claim.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State the correct inverse and explain the cancellation order.
parts.solution_html:
\[(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I\]
\[B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The factor next to B must be B⁻¹.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the numerical inverse with valid cancellation.

parts.label: b

stem_html: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). A real 2×2 matrix X satisfies \(XA=BX\), \(\det X=-8\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is 3.

parts.prompt_html: Write \(X=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\k & m\end{pmatrix}\) and obtain relations between its four entries from \(XA=BX\).
parts.solution_html:
\[XA=\begin{pmatrix}p & p + q\\k & k + m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BX=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\k + 2 p & m + 2 q\end{pmatrix}\]

The (1,2) entries give \(p+q=q\), so \(p=0\). The (2,2) entries give \(k+m=2q+m\), so \(k=2q\). The other two equations then hold automatically.
parts.hint_html: Do not attempt to cancel matrices across different sides of X.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all possible matrices \(X\).
parts.solution_html:
The diagonal-sum condition gives \(m=3\). The determinant is now \(-2q^2\), so \(-2q^2=-8\) gives \(q=\pm2\). The relation \(k=2q\) fixes the corresponding sign of k.

\[X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2\\4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -2\\-4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Keep the signs of k and q linked.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the diagonal condition to find m.
Give both complete matrices with consistent signs.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why multiplying \(XA=BX\) by inverses does not give \(A=B\).
parts.answer_html: It gives \(A=X^{-1}BX\), which need not equal B.
parts.solution_html: X is invertible because its determinant is −8. Premultiplying by \(X^{-1}\) yields \(A=X^{-1}BX\). The two X-factors are not adjacent, so they cannot simply be cancelled.
parts.hint_html: Matrix factors cannot be moved past B without justification.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the correctly rearranged equation and explain the invalid cancellation.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\det A\) and state precisely when \(A^{-1}\) exists.
parts.solution_html:
Expanding along the first column leaves an upper-triangular \(2\times2\) determinant.

\[\det A=3\begin{vmatrix}t&4\\0&2\end{vmatrix}=6t\]

The determinant is non-zero exactly when \(t\ne0\).
parts.hint_html: Use the zeros in the first column.

marking_points.criterion_html: Expand the determinant using a suitable row or column.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For the permitted values of \(t\), find \(A^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
The cofactor matrix is

\[\begin{pmatrix}2 t & 0 & 0\\- 2 t & 6 & 0\\2 t & -12 & 3 t\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose it and divide by \(6t\).

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

Multiplication on either side by \(A\) gives \(I_3\).
parts.hint_html: The inverse is upper triangular, or use the cofactor method.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find the cofactors or set up the upper-triangular inverse.
Give the complete inverse with its factor.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: A matrix \(X\) satisfies \(AX=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(X\) in terms of \(t\), and find the value of \(t\) for which the sum of the entries in the second row of \(X\) is \(-2\).
parts.solution_html:
Multiply on the left by \(A^{-1}\); the order cannot be reversed.

\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The second-row sum is \(-1/t\). Thus \(-1/t=-2\), giving \(t=1/2\), which is permitted.
parts.hint_html: Premultiply by the inverse and only then use the row-sum condition.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(A\) is non-singular for every real \(t\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=t(-4t-6)-(-6t+6)=-4t^2-6\]

Since \(t^2\ge0\), the determinant is at most \(-6\) and can never be zero.
parts.hint_html: A negative sum of a square and a positive constant cannot be zero.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain why it is non-zero for every real t.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: It is also known that \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - \dfrac{1}{10} & - \dfrac{3}{10}\\0 & \dfrac{1}{10} & \dfrac{3}{10}\\-2 & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(t\).
parts.solution_html: Use entry (1,3) of \(AA^{-1}=I\). It gives \(-3t/10+3/10=0\), hence \(t=1\). Substitution verifies the full identity.
parts.hint_html: Choose an off-diagonal entry of AA⁻¹ that has only two non-zero terms.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(A^{-1}\), showing your determinant and cofactor calculation.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=1(6)-1(4-1)=3\]

The cofactor matrix is

\[\begin{pmatrix}6 & -3 & -3\\-2 & 2 & 1\\1 & -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Transposing this matrix and dividing by 3 gives

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the \(3\times2\) matrix \(X\) such that \(AX=C\).
parts.solution_html:
Premultiply by \(A^{-1}\). Each column is treated by the same multiplication.

\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}2 & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\7 & 1\\-1 & 5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\2 & 0\\-1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

Direct multiplication of \(AX\) recovers both columns of \(C\).
parts.hint_html: Do not switch the order of A⁻¹ and C.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Verify that \(AB=\operatorname{diag}(3,6,3)\).
parts.solution_html:
Multiplying each row of A by each column of B gives

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0 & 0\\0 & 6 & 0\\0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Check the off-diagonal zeros as well as the diagonal entries.

marking_points.criterion_html: Verify all entries of the diagonal product.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Use part (a) to find \(A^{-1}\) without a new cofactor calculation.
parts.solution_html:
Write \(D=\operatorname{diag}(3,6,3)\). From \(AB=D\), we have \(A(BD^{-1})=I\). Thus

\[A^{-1}=BD^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 & 2\\1 & 2 & -1\\-1 & 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{6} & 0\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Multiply AB=D on the right by D⁻¹.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(B^{-1}\), again using part (a).
parts.solution_html:
Multiplying \(AB=D\) on the left by \(D^{-1}\) gives \((D^{-1}A)B=I\). Hence

\[B^{-1}=D^{-1}A=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3} & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{6} & \dfrac{1}{6}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: This time the diagonal inverse must go on the left.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: State the values of \(t\) for which the inverse does not exist, and find \(A^{-1}\) for all other values.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=t(t-1)-2=(t-2)(t+1)\]

The inverse fails at \(t=-1,2\). Otherwise swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant.

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t - 1}{t^{2} - t - 2} & - \dfrac{2}{t^{2} - t - 2}\\- \dfrac{1}{t^{2} - t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} - t - 2}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Factor the determinant before using it as a denominator.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The sum of the diagonal entries of \(A^{-1}\) is 1. Find every possible value of \(t\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\frac{2t-1}{t^2-t-2}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^2-3t-1=0\]
\[t=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}2\]

Neither value is −1 or 2, so both are permitted.
parts.hint_html: Use the restrictions from part (a) when clearing the denominator.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(A^{-1}\), showing the determinant and cofactor matrix.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=2(1)-(-1)(1)+1(2)=5\]
\[C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 2\\3 & 2 & -4\\-1 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

The adjugate is \(C^{\mathsf T}\), so

\[A^{-1}=\frac15 C^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5} & - \dfrac{1}{5}\\- \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\\\dfrac{2}{5} & - \dfrac{4}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use the alternating signs in the cofactor matrix; transpose before dividing.

marking_points.criterion_html: Transpose and divide to obtain the inverse.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: A column \(v\) satisfies \(Av=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(v\).
parts.solution_html: \[v=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{7}{5}\\- \dfrac{3}{5}\\\dfrac{26}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Premultiply by the inverse already found.
parts.label: b

stem_html: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & p & 2\\0 & 2 & 1\\1 & 0 & q\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}8 & -12 & -1\\1 & 2 & -1\\-2 & 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). It is known that \(AB=cI_3\) for a real number \(c\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(p,q,c\).
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}p + 4 & 2 p - 6 & 3 - p\\0 & 7 & 0\\8 - 2 q & 3 q - 12 & 2 q - 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Entry (1,2) must be zero, giving \(2p-6=0\) and \(p=3\). Entry (3,1) gives \(8-2q=0\), so \(q=4\). Every diagonal entry is then 7, hence \(c=7\). All other off-diagonal entries also vanish.
parts.hint_html: Use off-diagonal entries first, since c does not appear in them.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Deduce \(A^{-1}\) and find \(\det B\).
parts.solution_html: Since \(AB=7I\), \(A(B/7)=I\). Therefore \(A^{-1}=B/7\). Also \(\det A=7\), so \(7\det B=\det(7I_3)=7^3\), giving \(\det B=49\).
parts.hint_html: The determinant of 7I₃ is 7³, not 7.

marking_points.criterion_html: Divide the known factor by 7 to obtain the inverse.
Find det B=49 with the correct dimension factor.

parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
The determinants are 1 and 2 respectively. The cofactor matrices are

\[C_A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2 & 7\\0 & 1 & -3\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[C_B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-1 & 2 & 0\\2 & -4 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose each cofactor matrix and divide by its determinant:

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-2 & 1 & 0\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} & 1\\0 & 1 & -2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The (3,1) entry of \(A^{-1}\) accounts for the interaction between the two sub-diagonal entries; it is not obtained by merely changing a sign.
parts.hint_html: Exploit triangular structure but verify every off-diagonal entry.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Hence find \((AB)^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html: \[(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} & 1\\0 & 1 & -2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-2 & 1 & 0\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{17}{2} & - \dfrac{7}{2} & 1\\-16 & 7 & -2\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The inverse of B comes first in the product.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State \(\det((AB)^{-1})\) without expanding another determinant.
parts.solution_html: \[\det((AB)^{-1})=\frac1{\det A\det B}=\frac12\]
parts.hint_html: Use the product and inverse determinant rules.
parts.label: c

stem_html: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}k + 1 & 2 k\\1 & k\end{pmatrix}\). A matrix is called symmetric when it equals its transpose.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(A^{-1}\) and state its restrictions.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=k(k+1)-2k=k(k-1)\]
\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{k - 1} & - \dfrac{2}{k - 1}\\- \dfrac{1}{k^{2} - k} & \dfrac{k + 1}{k^{2} - k}\end{pmatrix}\]

The two zero-determinant values must be excluded.
parts.hint_html: First find k(k−1).
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the value of \(k\) for which \(A^{-1}\) is symmetric, and give that inverse.
parts.solution_html:
For a 2×2 matrix, symmetry requires its two off-diagonal entries to agree. Since the determinant is non-zero,

\[-2k=-1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\frac12\]

This is an allowed value. Substituting gives

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2 & 4\\4 & -6\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Equate only the off-diagonal entries, without forgetting the restrictions.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=1\]
\[C_A=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 & -1\\4 & -1 & -2\\-2 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose the cofactor matrix to obtain

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 4 & -2\\-1 & -1 & 1\\-1 & -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The determinant is 1, but the transpose of the cofactor matrix is still essential.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(X\) such that \(AX=C\).
parts.solution_html: \[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\-1 & 0\\3 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Premultiply by A⁻¹.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The entries in the first row of \(C\) are both increased by 1, forming \(C_1\). Without recomputing the entire product, find \(Y\) such that \(AY=C_1\).
parts.solution_html:
Subtract the two equations: \(A(Y-X)=C_1-C\). Thus

\[Y-X=A^{-1}(C_1-C)=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\-1 & -1\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

Each column of the change is the first column of \(A^{-1}\). Add this to X to get

\[Y=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\-2 & -1\\2 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The change in each output column is (1,0,0)ᵀ.

marking_points.criterion_html: Express the update as A⁻¹ times the change.
Give the update using the first column of A⁻¹.

parts.label: c

stem_html: The matrices \(A,B,C\) are non-singular 3×3 matrices. Their determinants are 2, −3 and 5 respectively.

parts.prompt_html: Prove, by showing the required cancellations, that \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
\[A B(CC^{-1})B^{-1}A^{-1}=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I\]
\[C^{-1}B^{-1}(A^{-1}A)BC=C^{-1}(B^{-1}B)C=I\]

Both products are I, so the claimed matrix is the inverse.
parts.hint_html: Regroup adjacent inverse pairs without interchanging factors.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use associativity to cancel the forward product.

parts.label: a

parts.solution_html:
\[\det(ABC)=2(-3)(5)=-30\]
\[\det(2ABC)=2^3(-30)=-240\]

The determinant of the inverse is the reciprocal, hence \(-1/240\).
parts.hint_html: Multiplying a 3×3 matrix by 2 multiplies its determinant by 8.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Verify algebraically that \(A^{-1}+B^{-1}=B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1}\). Hence express \((A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\) using \(A,B\) and \((A+B)^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
\[B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1}=B^{-1}AA^{-1}+B^{-1}BA^{-1}=B^{-1}+A^{-1}\]

Here \(\det(A+B)=8\ne0\), so every factor is invertible. Reverse the order on taking the inverse:

\[(B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1})^{-1}=A(A+B)^{-1}B\]
parts.hint_html: Expand the supplied factorisation without commuting any factors.

marking_points.criterion_html: Invert the three factors in reverse order.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \((A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\) numerically.
parts.solution_html:
\[A+B=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(A+B)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{8} & - \dfrac{1}{8}\\- \dfrac{1}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[A(A+B)^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{4} & \dfrac{1}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{4} & \dfrac{3}{4}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use the factorisation from part (a).
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State the area multiplier of the plane transformation represented by this matrix.
parts.solution_html: \[\left|\frac{\det A\det B}{\det(A+B)}\right|=\frac{2\cdot2}{8}=\frac12\]
parts.hint_html: Use the determinant of the product expression.
parts.label: c

stem_html: The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\0 & 1 & 3\\2 & 5 & t\end{pmatrix}\) depends on the real number \(t\).

parts.prompt_html: Find the value of \(t\) for which \(A\) is singular.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=(t-15)-2(-6)-2=t-5\]

Thus the only singular value is \(t=5\).
parts.hint_html: Expand along the first row.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For that value of \(t\), find \(u,v\) such that \(A\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) is the zero column. Explain why this rules out an inverse.
parts.solution_html:
The second component is \(v-3\), so \(v=3\). The first is \(u+2v-1\), giving \(u=-5\). The last component is then \(-10+15-5=0\).

If an inverse existed, multiplying \(A(-5,3,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0\) by it would imply the non-zero column \((-5,3,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) was zero, a contradiction.
parts.hint_html: Use the second component first; all three must vanish.

marking_points.criterion_html: Equate components of the product to zero.
Assume an inverse and premultiply the zero-product equation.
Identify the contradiction with a non-zero column.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find every value of \(t\) for which \(A\) is singular.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=t(t^2-1)-t=t(t^2-2)\]

Setting this equal to zero gives \(t=0,\sqrt2,-\sqrt2\).
parts.hint_html: Factor the determinant completely.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: When \(t=\sqrt2\), find a non-zero column \(v\) with first entry 1 such that \(Av=0\). Explain why \(A^{-1}\) cannot be used to solve this equation.
parts.solution_html:
Write \(v=(1,u,w)^{\mathsf T}\). The first row gives \(u=-\sqrt2\); the third gives \(w=1\). The middle row gives \(1-2+1=0\), so all three components vanish.

The determinant is zero, so \(A^{-1}\) does not exist. Multiplying by a supposed inverse would also contradict \(v\ne0\).
parts.hint_html: Use the first and third components and verify the middle one.

marking_points.criterion_html: Connect the zero determinant to the lack of an inverse.
Explain why the inverse method is invalid here.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all values of \(t\) for which \(A^{-1}\) exists.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=3\{t(t+1)-2\}=3(t+2)(t-1)\]

The inverse exists exactly when this is non-zero.
parts.hint_html: Expand along the last row.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For such \(t\), find \(A^{-1}\).
parts.answer_html: \[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t + 1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & - \dfrac{1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{- 2 t - 2}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\- \dfrac{2}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{4}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.solution_html:
The cofactors are

\[\begin{pmatrix}3 t + 3 & -6 & 0\\-3 & 3 t & 0\\- 2 t - 2 & 4 & t^{2} + t - 2\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose and divide by \(3(t+2)(t-1)\).

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t + 1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & - \dfrac{1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{- 2 t - 2}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\- \dfrac{2}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{4}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Keep the determinant factorised while simplifying.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use cofactors or a valid inverse calculation.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all real \(t\) for which \(\det(A^{-1})=1/12\).
parts.solution_html:
Computing the determinant of the inverse in part (b) gives \(1/[3(t+2)(t-1)]\). Hence

\[3(t+2)(t-1)=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(t-2)(t+3)=0\]

Thus t=2 or t=−3; both solutions avoid \(-2,1\).
parts.hint_html: Check both roots against the excluded values.
parts.label: c

stem_html: The matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t + 1 & t - 2\\2 t + 1 & 2 t - 1\end{pmatrix}\) maps a triangle of area 4 onto a triangle of area 12.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\det M\) in terms of \(t\).
parts.solution_html: \[\det M=(t+1)(2t-1)-(t-2)(2t+1)=4t+1\]
parts.hint_html: Expand both products before subtracting.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all possible real values of \(t\).
parts.solution_html:
\[4|4t+1|=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4t+1=3\ \text{or}\ 4t+1=-3\]

The resulting values are \(1/2\) and \(-1\). Both are non-singular.
parts.hint_html: Area uses the absolute determinant, so there are two sign cases.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For the negative value of \(t\), find \(M^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -3\\-1 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det M=-3\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\- \dfrac{1}{3} & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Substitute the chosen parameter before inverting.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the inverse formula on the correct numerical matrix.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(\det A=(t-1)^2(t+2)\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=t(t^2-1)-(t-1)+(1-t)=t^3-3t+2\]
\[t^3-3t+2=(t-1)(t^2+t-2)=(t-1)^2(t+2)\]
parts.hint_html: Expand along one row, then factor the cubic.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State all singular values and find the range of \(t\) for which \(\det(A^{-1})>0\).
parts.solution_html: For other t, \(\det(A^{-1})=1/[(t-1)^2(t+2)]\). The squared factor is strictly positive when \(t\ne1\), so the sign is the sign of \(t+2\). Require \(t>-2\) and exclude \(t=1\).
parts.hint_html: The repeated factor does not change sign, but its zero is still forbidden.
parts.label: b

stem_html: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - a & b\\a & 1 & 0\\- b & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(a,b\) are real.

parts.prompt_html: Prove that \(A\) is non-singular for all real \(a,b\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\det A=1-(-a)(a)+b(b)=1+a^2+b^2\]

Both squares are non-negative, so the determinant cannot vanish.
parts.hint_html: Expand along the first row and look for a sum of squares.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the largest possible value of \(\det(A^{-1})\) and state when it occurs.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det(A^{-1})=\frac1{1+a^2+b^2}\le1\]

Equality requires both squares to be zero, so \(a=b=0\).
parts.hint_html: Minimise the positive denominator.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Given \(a=1\) and \(\det A=6\), find \(b\).
parts.solution_html: \[1+1+b^2=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b^2=4\]
parts.hint_html: Keep both real square roots.
parts.label: c

stem_html: The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & p & 0\\0 & 2 & 1\\3 & 0 & q\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant 12. The entry in row 1, column 1 of \(A^{-1}\) is \(\frac12\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(p\) and \(q\) without calculating the complete inverse.
parts.solution_html:
The (1,1) cofactor is \(2q\). The inverse entry therefore gives

\[\frac{2q}{12}=\frac12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=3\]

Expanding the determinant of A gives \(2q+3p\). Hence \(6+3p=12\) and \(p=2\).
parts.hint_html: Use the cofactor formula for just the specified inverse entry.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: \[\det(3A^{-1})=3^3\det(A^{-1})=\frac{27}{12}=\frac94\]
parts.hint_html: There are three rows, so the scalar contributes 3³.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the correct scalar and inverse rules.

parts.label: b

stem_html: A triangle of area 5 is transformed into a triangle of area 15 by \(M=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2\\3 & k\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.prompt_html: Find every real value of \(k\).
parts.solution_html:
\[\det M=k^2-6,\qquad 5|k^2-6|=15\]

If \(k^2-6=3\), then \(k=\pm3\). If \(k^2-6=-3\), then \(k=\pm\sqrt3\). All four give non-zero determinant.
parts.hint_html: Area does not determine the sign of the determinant.

marking_points.criterion_html: Calculate det M and use the area relation.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For each class of values, state \(\det(M^{-1})\) and the area multiplier of the inverse transformation.
parts.answer_html: For \(k=\pm3\), the inverse determinant is \(1/3\). For \(k=\pm\sqrt3\), it is \(-1/3\). The inverse area multiplier is \(1/3\) in every case.
parts.solution_html: The original determinant is 3 for \(k=\pm3\) and −3 for \(k=\pm\sqrt3\). Hence the inverse determinants are \(1/3\) and \(-1/3\), respectively. Their absolute values are both \(1/3\).
parts.hint_html: Separate the signed determinant from the positive area multiplier.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(AB\) and its determinant.
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(AB)=3(-1)-1(1)=-4\]
parts.hint_html: AB has order 2×2.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(BA\) and show that it is singular.
parts.solution_html:
\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 2 & 0\\1 & 2 & 2\\0 & -1 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(BA)=2\begin{vmatrix}2&2\\-1&-2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\0&-2\end{vmatrix}=2(-2)-2(-2)=0\]
parts.hint_html: BA has order 3×3, so evaluate that determinant separately.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why these results do not contradict the rule \(\det(AB)=\det A\det B\).
parts.answer_html: That rule requires square factors of the same order; A and B are rectangular.
parts.solution_html: Neither det A nor det B is defined here. The two square products even have different orders, so the square-factor determinant theorem cannot be applied to these factors.
parts.hint_html: Check the hypotheses of the determinant rule.

marking_points.criterion_html: State why the rule is not applicable.

parts.label: c

stem_html: A non-singular 3×3 matrix A has rows \(u,v,w\) and determinant −2. A matrix B has rows \(3u,u+v,2v-w\), in that order.

parts.prompt_html: Find a numerical matrix \(K\) such that \(B=KA\).
parts.solution_html:
Left multiplication takes combinations of the rows of A. The coefficients of u,v,w in the three new rows are \((3,0,0),(1,1,0),(0,2,-1)\). These form the rows of K.

\[K=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0 & 0\\1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The row coefficients belong in the rows of a left multiplier.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use a left multiplier to form row combinations.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\det B\) and \(\det(B^{-1}A)\).
parts.solution_html:
K is triangular, with determinant \(3(1)(-1)=-3\). Thus \(\det B=(-3)(-2)=6\). Consequently,

\[\det(B^{-1}A)=\frac{\det A}{\det B}=-\frac26=-\frac13\]
parts.hint_html: Use the determinant product rule, including its signs.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: A student proposes \(B^{-1}=K^{-1}A^{-1}\). State the correct expression.
parts.solution_html: Since \(B=KA\), the inverse reverses those two factors.
parts.hint_html: Reverse the order of the actual product KA.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Describe both transformations represented in this product and state their order.
parts.answer_html: A shear with the y-axis fixed, \((1,0)\mapsto(1,k)\), followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(2\theta\) about the origin.
parts.solution_html: The right-hand matrix acts first. Its coordinate rule is \((x,y)\mapsto(x,kx+y)\), which fixes every point on the y-axis. The left-hand matrix is the standard rotation matrix.
parts.hint_html: For column vectors the right-hand factor acts first.

marking_points.criterion_html: Identify a shear fixing the y-axis with the correct example image.
Identify the rotation angle, direction and centre.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Express \(M^{-1}\) as a product of two non-identity matrices.
parts.solution_html:
Undo the rotation first, then the shear. Inverse factors appear in reverse order:

\[(RS)^{-1}=S^{-1}R^{-1}\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- k & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Reverse the order and invert each factor.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the condition relating \(k\) and \(\tan\theta\) for \(M-I\) to be singular. Justify any division used.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}- k \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} + \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\k \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} + \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(M-I)=2-2\cos2\theta+k\sin2\theta=0\]
\[4\sin^2\theta+2k\sin\theta\cos\theta=0\]

Here \(\sin\theta>0\). If \(\cos\theta=0\), the left side is 4, not zero. Division by \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) is therefore valid and gives \(2\tan\theta+k=0\).
parts.hint_html: Expand det(M−I), then use double-angle identities.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Take \(k=-2\) and \(\theta=\pi/4\). Find all invariant points and show that they form a line.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M\binom{x}{y}=\binom{2x-y}{x}=\binom{x}{y}\]

Both equations reduce to \(y=x\). Conversely every point \((x,x)\) is unchanged, so this is the complete fixed-point line.
parts.hint_html: Invariant points satisfy Mv=v, not just Y=mX.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the entire line y=x and verify the converse.

parts.label: d

stem_html: A rotation anticlockwise through \(\theta\) about the origin is followed by a stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(3+2\sqrt2\). Let \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

parts.prompt_html: Write the matrix \(M\) representing the combined transformation.
parts.solution_html:
The rotation is first, so its matrix is on the right of the stretch matrix.

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 \sqrt{2} + 3 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\left(2 \sqrt{2} + 3\right) \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \left(2 \sqrt{2} + 3\right) \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use stretch × rotation, not rotation × stretch.

marking_points.criterion_html: Place the factors in the correct order.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all values of \(\theta\) for which there is exactly one invariant line through the origin. Give that line for each angle.
parts.solution_html:
Write \(h=3+2\sqrt2\). For \(y=mx\), the image coordinates satisfy \(Y=mX\) exactly when

\[h\sin\theta\,m^2-(h-1)\cos\theta\,m+\sin\theta=0\]

For \(0<\theta<\pi\), the vertical line is not invariant because its image has x-coordinate \(-h\sin\theta\,y\). The slope equation has exactly one real root when

\[\Delta=(h-1)^2\cos^2\theta-4h\sin^2\theta=4h(2\cos^2\theta-1)=0\]

Thus \(\theta=\pi/4,3\pi/4\). The repeated slope is \((h-1)\cos\theta/(2h\sin\theta)\), equal to \(\sqrt2-1\) and \(-(\sqrt2-1)\) respectively. At \(\theta=0,\pi\) both coordinate axes are invariant, so the endpoints are excluded.
parts.hint_html: Use the slope discriminant, but check the vertical line and both endpoint angles separately.

marking_points.criterion_html: Exclude θ=0 and π because each has two invariant axes.
Give the correct invariant line at each angle.

parts.label: b

stem_html: A stretch parallel to the y-axis with positive factor \(a\) is followed by a shear fixing the y-axis and sending \((1,0)\) to \((1,b)\), where \(b>0\). Their combined matrix is \(M\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M\).
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & a\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & a\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Apply the stretch first.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the matrix which maps the image of the unit square back onto the original square, with corresponding vertices restored.
parts.solution_html:
Restoring corresponding points requires the inverse, not merely a matrix giving the same area.

\[\det M=a\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- \dfrac{b}{a} & \dfrac{1}{a}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use the inverse matrix.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The image of the unit square has area 4. The line \(y=-2x\) is invariant. Find \(a\) and \(b\).
parts.solution_html: The area scale factor is \(|\det M|=a\), so \(a=4\). A point \((x,-2x)\) maps to \((x,(b-2a)x)\). To stay on the same line, \(b-2a=-2\), hence \(b=6\).
parts.hint_html: Use the determinant for area and substitute a general point from the line.

marking_points.criterion_html: Transform a general point on the specified line.

parts.label: c

stem_html: The transformation \(T_k\) has matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\k & 2 k\end{pmatrix}\), where \(k\in\mathbb R\).

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(M\) is singular for every \(k\) and find the equation of the line containing all image points.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det M=2k-2k=0\]
\[X=x+2y,\qquad Y=k(x+2y)=kX\]

Every point on \(Y=kX\) occurs: choose \((x,y)=(X,0)\).
parts.hint_html: Factor the second image coordinate.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant points, treating \(k=0\) and \(k\ne0\) separately.
parts.solution_html: The fixed-point equations are \(x+2y=x\) and \(k(x+2y)=y\). The first gives \(y=0\) and the second becomes \(kx=0\). If k=0, the whole x-axis is fixed; if k is non-zero, only the origin is fixed.
parts.hint_html: Solve Mv=v, not Mv=0.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all real \(k\) for which \(M^2=M\). Explain geometrically what happens on applying \(T_k\) twice in that case.
parts.solution_html:
\[M^2=(1+2k)M\]

As \(M\ne0\), equality with \(M\) requires \(k=0\). For this value the first application places every point on the x-axis, and every point on that axis is fixed, so the second application changes nothing.
parts.hint_html: Calculate M² directly.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Describe the transformations represented by \(A\) and \(B\) fully.
parts.answer_html: A: shear fixing the x-axis, \((0,1)\mapsto(2,1)\). B: shear fixing the y-axis, \((1,0)\mapsto(1,1/4)\).
parts.solution_html: The coordinate rules are \(A:(x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,y)\) and \(B:(x,y)\mapsto(x,x/4+y)\). These identify the fixed axes and shear amounts.
parts.hint_html: Use a point on each fixed axis and one point off it.

marking_points.criterion_html: Give the type, fixed axis and example image for A.
Give the type, fixed axis and example image for B.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Show that a triangle and its image under \(AB\) have equal areas.
parts.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{2} & 2\\\dfrac{1}{4} & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(AB)=\frac32-\frac12=1\]

The area multiplier is the absolute determinant, hence 1.
parts.hint_html: Multiply AB or evaluate its determinant directly.

marking_points.criterion_html: Compute AB and its determinant, or justify an equivalent method.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant lines through the origin under \(AB\).
parts.solution_html:
\[X=\frac32x+2y,\qquad Y=\frac14x+y\]

For \(y=mx\), impose \(Y=mX\):

\[\frac14+m=m\left(\frac32+2m\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8m^2+2m-1=(4m-1)(2m+1)=0\]

Thus \(m=1/4,-1/2\). The vertical line is not invariant because \((0,y)\mapsto(2y,y)\).
parts.hint_html: Check x=0 separately from y=mx.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the line containing all image points and find all points mapped to \((3,6)\).
parts.solution_html:
\[X=2x-y,\qquad Y=4x-2y=2X\]

Every value of X is possible, so the full image is \(Y=2X\). For image \((3,6)\), the condition is \(2x-y=3\), giving the stated family.
parts.hint_html: The two image equations are dependent.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant points.
parts.solution_html: The equations \(2x-y=x\) and \(4x-2y=y\) give \(y=x\) and then \(4x=3x\). Thus \(x=y=0\).
parts.hint_html: Fixed points must satisfy both Mv=v equations.

marking_points.criterion_html: Set up and solve the fixed-point equations.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Calculate \(M^2\) and explain the result in terms of the image line from part (a).
parts.solution_html:
\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

The first image lies on \(Y=2X\). Applying M to any point \((X,2X)\) produces \((0,0)\). Therefore two applications send the entire plane to the origin.
parts.hint_html: Apply the map to a general point on its image line.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain why the image line collapses on the second application.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M^{-1}\) and explain why every image point has exactly one preimage.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det M=4-3=1\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

For each image column w, the unique preimage is \(M^{-1}w\). If two preimages had the same image, premultiplying by the inverse would make them equal.
parts.hint_html: A non-zero determinant gives a reversible map.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain existence and uniqueness of the preimage.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of the image of the line \(y=x+1\). Use \((X,Y)\) for image coordinates.
parts.solution_html:
Substitute \(x=2X-3Y\) and \(y=-X+2Y\) from the inverse into \(y=x+1\).

\[-X+2Y=2X-3Y+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5Y-3X=1\]
parts.hint_html: Substitute inverse coordinates into the original line.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use inverse coordinates or a correct parameterisation.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant lines through the origin.
parts.solution_html:
\[1+2m=m(2+3m)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3m^2=1\]

The lines are \(y=x/\sqrt3\) and \(y=-x/\sqrt3\). The vertical line is not invariant, because \((0,y)\mapsto(3y,2y)\).
parts.hint_html: Use Y=mX and then check x=0.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Explain why \(M\binom12=\binom12\) and \(M\binom{-2}{1}=\binom2{-1}\). Hence find \(M\).
parts.solution_html:
The first vector lies on the mirror line and is fixed. The second is perpendicular to it, since \(1(-2)+2(1)=0\), and reflection reverses that vector. Thus

\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5}\\- \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{5} & \dfrac{4}{5}\\\dfrac{4}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use one direction along the mirror and one perpendicular to it.

marking_points.criterion_html: Form a matrix equation from the two images.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the image of \((5,0)\) and verify that applying the reflection a second time returns this point.
parts.solution_html:
\[M\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Multiply the image column by the same matrix.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State the area multiplier.
parts.solution_html: The determinant is −1, so its absolute value is 1.
parts.hint_html: Reflections preserve area.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Describe fully the shear represented by each matrix.
parts.answer_html: S fixes the x-axis and sends \((0,1)\) to \((2,1)\). T fixes the y-axis and sends \((1,0)\) to \((1,-1)\).
parts.solution_html: The coordinate rules are \(S:(x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,y)\) and \(T:(x,y)\mapsto(x,y-x)\). These identify the fixed axes and shear directions.
parts.hint_html: Read the image coordinates from each product with (x,y)ᵀ.

marking_points.criterion_html: Describe S with fixed axis and example image.
Describe T with fixed axis and example image.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(ST\) and \(TS\). Give the two different images of \((1,1)\) under these composites.
parts.solution_html:
\[ST=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 2\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[TS=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[ST\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[TS\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The rightmost shear acts first.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Show that applying either composite twice has the same geometrical effect. Describe this effect fully.
parts.solution_html:
\[(ST)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(TS)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix −I₂ sends \((x,y)\) to \((-x,-y)\). It is a rotation through \(\pi\) about the origin.
parts.hint_html: Square each product, then recognise the coordinate rule.
parts.label: c

stem_html: A reflection in the x-axis is followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\pi/3\) about the origin.

parts.prompt_html: Find the matrix \(M\) of the composite transformation.
parts.solution_html: \[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Apply the reflection first, so its matrix is on the right.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the line of invariant points.
parts.solution_html:
Solve \(M\binom xy=\binom xy\). The first component gives

\[\frac12x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}y=x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\sqrt3 y\]

The second component gives the same condition.
parts.hint_html: Invariant points satisfy Mv=v, not just that the image is parallel to v.

marking_points.criterion_html: Set the image equal to the original point.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Show that the composite is a reflection in this line, not merely a transformation fixing the line.
parts.answer_html: It fixes the direction \((\sqrt3,1)\) and reverses the perpendicular direction \((-1,\sqrt3)\).
parts.solution_html:
\[M\begin{pmatrix}-1\\\sqrt{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\- \sqrt{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

This is the negative of the input vector. Every point can be resolved into components along these two perpendicular directions. M leaves the parallel component unchanged and reverses the perpendicular component: exactly reflection in \(y=x/\sqrt3\).
parts.hint_html: Check what happens to a perpendicular direction as well.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain why the two component rules identify the reflection.

parts.label: c

stem_html: A transformation first stretches parallel to the x-axis with factor 2, then rotates anticlockwise through \(\pi/2\) about the origin, and finally applies a shear fixing the y-axis and mapping \((1,0)\) to \((1,3)\).

parts.prompt_html: Find the matrix \(M\) of the transformation.
parts.solution_html: \[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\2 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Write the matrices in reverse chronological order.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M^{-1}\) and describe the operations of the inverse transformation in order.
parts.answer_html:
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

Shear fixing the y-axis with \((1,0)\mapsto(1,-3)\); clockwise rotation through \(\pi/2\) about the origin; stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(1/2\).
parts.solution_html:
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-3 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

The rightmost factor undoes the last shear first. Then undo the rotation and finally the stretch.
parts.hint_html: Reverse both the factors and the physical operations.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the preimage of \((4,-2)\).
parts.solution_html: \[\binom xy=M^{-1}\binom4{-2}=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use the inverse, not the forward map.

marking_points.criterion_html: Apply the inverse to the given output.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of the image of the line \(x=2\).
parts.solution_html: The coordinate rule is \(X=x+2y\), \(Y=3x+4y\). Eliminating y gives \(Y-2X=x\). Thus the image of \(x=2\) is \(Y-2X=2\). Since M is non-singular, this is the whole image line.
parts.hint_html: Eliminate y from the two output coordinates.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of the line whose image is \(2X-Y=5\).
parts.solution_html: \[2(x+2y)-(3x+4y)=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=-5\]
parts.hint_html: For a preimage, substitute the forward rule into the output equation.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the input point whose image is the intersection of \(Y-2X=2\) and \(X+Y=8\).
parts.solution_html:
The output intersection is \((X,Y)=(2,6)\). Multiplication by \(M^{-1}\) gives

\[\binom xy=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Find the output intersection before applying the inverse.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant points.
parts.solution_html: The rule is \((X,Y)=(3x,y)\). Equality with \((x,y)\) requires \(3x=x\), so \(x=0\), with y arbitrary.
parts.hint_html: A fixed point must have unchanged coordinates.

marking_points.criterion_html: Set image coordinates equal to input coordinates.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant straight lines, including those not passing through the origin.
parts.solution_html: For a non-vertical line \(y=mx+c\), use \(x=X/3\) and \(y=Y\) to obtain \(Y=(m/3)X+c\). Equality with the original line requires \(m/3=m\), hence \(m=0\), with any c. A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=3d\), so is invariant only when \(d=0\).
parts.hint_html: Consider non-vertical and vertical lines separately.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Explain why \(y=2\) is invariant but is not a line of invariant points.
parts.answer_html: Its points stay on the same line, but only (0,2) is fixed.
parts.solution_html: A point \((x,2)\) maps to \((3x,2)\), which is on \(y=2\). For \(x\ne0\), the position changes.
parts.hint_html: Distinguish setwise preservation from pointwise preservation.

marking_points.criterion_html: Explain the distinction with the actual coordinate rule.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Describe the transformation fully and find its invariant points.
parts.answer_html: Reflection in \(y=-x\); the invariant points are exactly those on this line.
parts.solution_html: The rule is \((X,Y)=(-y,-x)\). It fixes \((x,-x)\) and reverses the perpendicular direction \((1,1)\), so it is reflection in \(y=-x\). Setting the image equal to the input gives the same line.
parts.hint_html: Check the line y=−x and the perpendicular direction.

marking_points.criterion_html: Identify the reflection and its mirror line.
Give the full set of fixed points.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant straight lines.
parts.solution_html:
For a point on \(y=mx+c\), require \(Y=mX+c\). Substitution gives

\[-x=-m(mx+c)+c=-m^2x+c(1-m)\]

Therefore \(m^2=1\) and \(c(1-m)=0\). If \(m=1\), any c works. If \(m=-1\), then \(c=0\). A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to the horizontal line \(Y=-d\), so no vertical line is invariant.
parts.hint_html: A reflected line may remain the same set without being fixed point by point.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: State the only fixed point on \(y=x+6\).
parts.solution_html: Intersect \(y=x+6\) with the fixed-point line \(y=-x\). This gives \(2x=-6\) and the point \((-3,3)\).
parts.hint_html: A fixed point must also lie on the mirror line.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Explain the restriction \(t\ne-2\). Derive an equation for the gradient \(m\) of an invariant line through the origin.
parts.solution_html: The determinant is \(t+2\), so the restriction ensures a non-singular transformation. On \(y=mx\), the image is \(((t+m)x,(m-2)x)\). Requiring \(Y=mX\) gives \(m-2=m(t+m)\), and hence the equation. The vertical line is not invariant since \((0,y)\mapsto(y,y)\).
parts.hint_html: Treat the vertical line separately from y=mx.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Classify the permitted values of \(t\) giving no invariant line, exactly one invariant line, or two invariant lines through the origin.
parts.answer_html: None: \(1-2\sqrt2<t<1+2\sqrt2\). Exactly one: \(t=1\pm2\sqrt2\). Two: \(t<1-2\sqrt2\) or \(t>1+2\sqrt2\), with \(t=-2\) excluded.
parts.solution_html:
\[\Delta=(t-1)^2-8\]

The quadratic in m has zero, one or two real roots according as this discriminant is negative, zero or positive. Keep the original exclusion of \(t=-2\) in the positive-discriminant case.
parts.hint_html: Use the discriminant of the gradient equation, not det M.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant points for any permitted \(t\).
parts.solution_html: Since \(\det(M-I)=2\ne0\), the equation \((M-I)v=0\) has only \(v=0\): multiply by the inverse of M−I.
parts.hint_html: Fixed points satisfy (M−I)v=0.

marking_points.criterion_html: Justify that only the origin is fixed.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find every invariant line through the origin.
parts.solution_html: For \(y=mx\), the image is \((2x,(3-m)x)\). Thus \(3-m=2m\), so \(m=1\). In addition, \((0,y)\mapsto(0,-y)\), so the vertical line \(x=0\) is invariant. These exhaust the possible directions.
parts.hint_html: Do not assume that every line has a finite gradient.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Describe what happens to points on each of these lines and find all fixed points.
parts.answer_html: On \(y=x\), points are enlarged by factor 2 from the origin. On \(x=0\), points are reversed through the origin. Only the origin is fixed.
parts.solution_html:
\[M\binom xx=2\binom xx,\qquad M\binom0y=-\binom0y\]

Neither rule fixes a non-zero point. Alternatively, \(2x=x\) gives \(x=0\), then \(-y=y\) gives \(y=0\).
parts.hint_html: An invariant direction does not imply fixed points.

marking_points.criterion_html: State that only the origin is fixed.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all values of \(t\) for which the transformation has a line of invariant points.
parts.solution_html:
A non-zero fixed point solves \((M-I)v=0\), so M−I must be singular:

\[\det(M-I)=(t-1)(t-2)-6=(t-4)(t+1)=0\]

These two values will each produce a line, as verified next. Neither makes M singular: its determinants are −4 and 6 respectively.
parts.hint_html: Use det(M−I)=0, not det M=0.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: For each value, find the complete line of invariant points.
parts.solution_html: For \(t=-1\), the equations are \(-2x+2y=0\) and \(3x-3y=0\), giving \(y=x\). For \(t=4\), both equations reduce to \(3x+2y=0\). In each case a genuine line of solutions exists, not the whole plane.
parts.hint_html: Substitute each value before simplifying the two equations.

marking_points.criterion_html: Solve the fixed-point equations in each case.

parts.label: b

stem_html: A linear transformation sends \((1,1)\) to \((2,2)\) and \((1,-2)\) to \((-3,6)\).

parts.prompt_html: Find its matrix \(M\).
parts.solution_html:
\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\2 & 6\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\2 & 6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{5}{3}\\\dfrac{10}{3} & - \dfrac{4}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Build a matrix equation using the two input columns.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the correct inverse and multiplication order.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Without using a new matrix multiplication, find the image of \((2,-1)\).
parts.solution_html: The input is \((1,1)+(1,-2)\). Linearity gives the image \((2,2)+(-3,6)=(-1,8)\).
parts.hint_html: Add the two supplied input columns.

marking_points.criterion_html: Express the input as the sum of the supplied vectors.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The triangle has vertices \((0,0),(1,1),(1,-2)\). Find the area of its image, and state two invariant lines.
parts.solution_html: The original area is \(\frac12|1(-2)-1(1)|=\frac32\). Since \(|\det M|=6\), the image area is \(9\). Each supplied direction remains on the same line, so \(y=x\) and \(y=-2x\) are invariant.
parts.hint_html: Use the determinant for area and the supplied images for directions.

marking_points.criterion_html: Find the original area and area multiplier.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant points.
parts.solution_html: The rule is \((X,Y)=(x+ky,y)\). Fixed points require \(ky=0\). Since \(k\ne0\), precisely the x-axis is fixed.
parts.hint_html: Use the assumption k≠0.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant straight lines and justify that there are no others.
parts.solution_html:
On \(y=mx+c\), the equation \(Y=mX+c\) gives

\[mx+c=m(x+k(mx+c))+c\]

Comparing coefficients gives \(km^2=0\), hence \(m=0\); the constant c is unrestricted. A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=d+kY\), not a vertical line. Thus precisely the horizontal lines are invariant.
parts.hint_html: Check both finite-gradient and vertical lines.
parts.label: b

stem_html: A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor 2 and a stretch parallel to the y-axis with factor \(1/2\) are followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\theta\) about the origin, where \(0<\theta<\pi\).

parts.prompt_html: Find the composite matrix \(M\) and show that it preserves area.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \dfrac{\sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\\2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \dfrac{\cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

Each rotation has determinant 1, and the two stretches have product determinant \(2(1/2)=1\). The absolute determinant is therefore 1.
parts.hint_html: The rotation is applied last and appears on the left.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the value of \(\theta\) for which there is a line of invariant points.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det(M-I)=2-\frac52\cos\theta\]

A non-zero fixed point requires this determinant to vanish, so \(\cos\theta=4/5\). On the given interval this gives the single angle stated, with \(\sin\theta=3/5\).
parts.hint_html: Fixed points require a singular M−I.

marking_points.criterion_html: Select the unique angle in the given interval.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For this angle, find the fixed-point line and show that it is the only invariant line through the origin.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{8}{5} & - \dfrac{3}{10}\\\dfrac{6}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed-point equations reduce to \(2x-y=0\). For an invariant line \(y=mx\), the condition \(Y=mX\) simplifies to \((m-2)^2=0\). The vertical line is not invariant because the (1,2) entry of M is non-zero. Thus there is exactly one invariant direction, and its line is fixed pointwise.
parts.hint_html: Find fixed points first, then separately check all invariant directions.

marking_points.criterion_html: Exclude the vertical line and conclude uniqueness.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Describe the transformations in the correct order and find \(M\).
parts.answer_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}a b + 1 & a\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

First the shear T fixing the y-axis, then the shear S fixing the x-axis.
parts.solution_html:
T sends \((1,0)\) to \((1,b)\) and S sends \((0,1)\) to \((a,1)\). Since the right factor acts first, apply T then S.

\[ST=\begin{pmatrix}a b + 1 & a\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The product ST applies T first.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M^{-1}\) and the area multiplier of the transformation.
parts.solution_html:
\[\det M=1+ab-ab=1\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - a\\- b & a b + 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The area multiplier is \(|1|=1\).
parts.hint_html: Use det M before finding its inverse.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Classify the values of \(ab\) for which M has zero, one or two invariant lines through the origin.
parts.answer_html: Zero if \(-4<ab<0\); one if \(ab=-4\); two if \(ab<-4\) or \(ab>0\).
parts.solution_html:
For \(y=mx\), require \(b+m=m(1+ab+am)\). Thus

\[am^2+abm-b=0,\qquad\Delta=ab(ab+4)\]

Since \(a\ne0\), this is a genuine quadratic. Its discriminant is negative when ab lies strictly between −4 and 0, zero at ab=−4, and positive when ab is below −4 or above 0. The value \(ab=0\) is excluded by the question. The vertical line is not invariant because \((0,y)\mapsto(ay,y)\) and \(a\ne0\).
parts.hint_html: Classify the sign of the slope discriminant; do not add the excluded case ab=0.

marking_points.criterion_html: Deal with vertical lines and the excluded value ab=0.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: When \(a=2,b=-2\), find the invariant line and determine whether its non-zero points are fixed.
parts.solution_html: The slope equation is \(2(m-1)^2=0\), so the line is \(y=x\). On this line M sends each point to its negative, so only the origin is fixed.
parts.hint_html: An invariant line need not consist of invariant points.

marking_points.criterion_html: Show non-zero points are reversed, not fixed.

parts.label: d

stem_html: A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(a>0\) is followed by a shear fixing the x-axis and sending \((0,1)\) to \((b,1)\). Finally there is a reflection in \(y=x\). The combined matrix is \(M\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M\) in terms of \(a,b\).
parts.solution_html: \[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & b\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\a & b\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The reflection matrix is the leftmost factor.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The unit square has image area 6, and \((1,2)\) maps to \((2,10)\). Find \(a,b\).
parts.solution_html: Since \(\det M=-a\) and \(a>0\), the area gives \(a=6\). The second image coordinate gives \(a+2b=10\), hence \(b=2\).
parts.hint_html: Use a>0 after taking the absolute determinant.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the determinant and area to find a=6.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M^{-1}\) and describe the three operations that undo the original transformation, in the order applied.
parts.solution_html:
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{6}\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

First reflect in \(y=x\), then apply the shear fixing the x-axis with \((0,1)\mapsto(-2,1)\), then stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(1/6\). This reverses both the operations and their order.
parts.hint_html: Undo the last operation first.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant lines through the origin.
parts.solution_html: On \(y=mx\), the image is \((mx,(6+2m)x)\). Thus \(m^2-2m-6=0\), giving \(m=1\pm\sqrt7\). The vertical line maps onto \(Y=2X\), so is not invariant.
parts.hint_html: Use Y=mX and remember the vertical line.
parts.label: d

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of the line whose image is \(X+Y=8\).
parts.solution_html: Substitute \(X=y\) and \(Y=6x+2y\) into the desired image equation: \(y+6x+2y=8\).
parts.hint_html: This is a preimage question: substitute the forward coordinate rule.
parts.label: e

stem_html: Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\q & p\end{pmatrix}\), where \(p>q>0\). The point \((1,1)\) maps to \((5,5)\), and the image of the unit square has area 15.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(p,q\).
parts.solution_html:
The given image gives \(p+q=5\). Since \(p>q>0\), the determinant \((p-q)(p+q)\) is positive. Hence

\[(p-q)5=15\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p-q=3\]

Solving with \(p+q=5\) gives \(p=4,q=1\).
parts.hint_html: The inequalities allow you to remove the absolute value in the area equation.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant lines through the origin and all invariant points.
parts.solution_html:
For \(y=mx\), \(Y=mX\) gives \(1+4m=m(4+m)\), hence \(m^2=1\). The vertical line is not invariant, as \((0,y)\mapsto(y,4y)\). For fixed points,

\[3x+y=0,\qquad x+3y=0\]

Substitution gives \(x=y=0\).
parts.hint_html: Apply separate equations for invariant lines and invariant points.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Show that the image of the unit square is a rhombus but not a rectangle.
parts.answer_html: Adjacent side vectors are (4,1) and (1,4); both have length √17, but their scalar product is 8.
parts.solution_html: The vertices are \((0,0),(4,1),(5,5),(1,4)\). The two adjacent side lengths are both \(\sqrt{17}\), so all four sides of this parallelogram are equal. Their scalar product is \(4(1)+1(4)=8\ne0\), so the sides are not perpendicular and it is not a rectangle.
parts.hint_html: Use the two columns as adjacent side vectors.

marking_points.criterion_html: Show the angle is not a right angle.

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Find the matrix which maps this image back to the unit square.
parts.solution_html: \[M^{-1}=\frac1{15}\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Use the inverse, retaining the determinant factor.
parts.label: d

stem_html: For a real number \(t\), define \(M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{t^{2} + 1} & \dfrac{2 t}{t^{2} + 1}\\\dfrac{2 t}{t^{2} + 1} & \dfrac{t^{2} - 1}{t^{2} + 1}\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.prompt_html: By direct multiplication, show that \(M^2=I\) and deduce \(M^{-1}\).
parts.solution_html: The diagonal numerators of M² are \((1-t^2)^2+4t^2=(1+t^2)^2\). Each off-diagonal numerator is \(2t(1-t^2)+2t(t^2-1)=0\). Division by \((1+t^2)^2\) therefore gives I. Since \(M M=I\), its inverse is itself.
parts.hint_html: Calculate diagonal and off-diagonal entries symbolically.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(M\) represents reflection in \(y=tx\), including the case \(t=0\).
parts.answer_html: The direction (1,t) is fixed and the perpendicular direction (−t,1) is reversed.
parts.solution_html:
\[M\binom1t=\binom1t,\qquad M\binom{-t}1=-\binom{-t}1\]

The directions are perpendicular because \(1(-t)+t(1)=0\) and are independent for every real t. Thus M fixes the component along \(y=tx\) and reverses the perpendicular component. This is the defining reflection rule. When \(t=0\), M is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), reflection in the x-axis.
parts.hint_html: A proof that M²=I alone would not distinguish a reflection from other transformations.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
\[\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}=-\frac5{13}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^2=\frac94\]

The second coordinate \(2t/(1+t^2)=12/13>0\) forces \(t>0\). Therefore \(t=3/2\).
parts.hint_html: The first coordinate determines |t|; the second fixes its sign.

marking_points.criterion_html: Use the first coordinate to find t².

parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: For this value of \(t\), find the image of \((1,0)\) after 87 successive applications.
parts.solution_html: Since \(M^2=I\), \(M^{87}=(M^2)^{43}M=M\). Thus the image is the same as after one application.
parts.hint_html: Pair the applications using M²=I.
parts.label: d

parts.prompt_html: Find the complete set of invariant points.
parts.solution_html: The image is \((2x+y,y)\). It equals the input precisely when \(x+y=0\).
parts.hint_html: The second coordinate is already unchanged.

marking_points.criterion_html: Set the first coordinate equal to x.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all invariant straight lines, including those not through the origin.
parts.solution_html:
For \(y=mx+c\), the image is \(((2+m)x+c,mx+c)\). It lies on the same line exactly when

\[mx+c=m((2+m)x+c)+c\]

Comparing coefficients of x and constants gives \(m(m+1)=0\) and \(mc=0\). Thus \(m=0\) permits any c; \(m=-1\) requires \(c=0\). A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=2d+Y\), not a vertical line. Hence the list is complete.
parts.hint_html: Compare both the gradient and the constant term; then test vertical lines.

marking_points.criterion_html: Justify that there are no additional lines.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether there is any point which returns to its starting position after two applications of M but is not fixed after one application.
parts.solution_html:
\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Returning after two applications requires \(4x+3y=x\), hence \(x+y=0\). Every such point is already fixed by part (a). Therefore a two-step return without a one-step return is impossible.
parts.hint_html: Solve M²v=v and compare with the fixed-point set of M.

marking_points.criterion_html: Conclude that no point has exactly a two-step return.

parts.label: c

stem_html: A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(a>1\) is followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\theta\) about the origin, where \(0\le\theta\le\pi\). The composite matrix is M.

parts.prompt_html: Find \(M\) and write its inverse as a product of two standard transformation matrices.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\a \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

Undo the rotation first, then the stretch. Hence

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{a} & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The chronological order of the inverse transformations is reversed.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The image of the unit square has area 9. Find \(a\).
parts.solution_html: A rotation preserves area and the stretch multiplies it by \(a>1\). Equivalently \(|\det M|=a=9\).
parts.hint_html: Use the determinant, not the side lengths after rotation.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For this value of \(a\), find every \(\theta\) for which there is exactly one invariant line through the origin, and find that line in each case.
parts.solution_html:
For \(0<\theta<\pi\), a line \(y=mx\) is invariant when

\[\sin\theta\,m^2-8\cos\theta\,m+9\sin\theta=0\]

Exactly one finite gradient requires discriminant zero:

\[64\cos^2\theta-36\sin^2\theta=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\cos\theta=\pm\frac35\]

In both cases \(\sin\theta=4/5\). The repeated gradient is \(m=4\cos\theta/\sin\theta\), giving 3 and −3. The vertical line is not invariant in the open interval because \(\sin\theta\ne0\). At \(\theta=0,\pi\) the two coordinate axes are invariant, so those endpoints do not qualify.
parts.hint_html: Check the discriminant and the endpoint angles separately.
parts.label: c

parts.prompt_html: Take the acute angle from part (c). Find the image of \(y=3x+c\) and determine which of these lines are invariant.
parts.solution_html:
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{27}{5} & - \dfrac{4}{5}\\\dfrac{36}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

Substitution of \(y=3x+c\) gives \(X=3x-4c/5\) and \(Y=9x+3c/5\). Hence \(Y-3X=3c\). The original line and its image agree only when \(3c=c\), so \(c=0\).
parts.hint_html: The invariant direction is not sufficient: compare the intercepts too.
parts.label: d

parts.prompt_html: For the same acute angle, find all invariant points and describe the action on its invariant line.
parts.answer_html: Only the origin is fixed. On \(y=3x\), points are enlarged from the origin by factor 3.
parts.solution_html:
\[M\binom{x}{3x}=3\binom{x}{3x}\]

No non-zero point of that line is fixed. More generally, \(\det(M-I)=4\ne0\), so the fixed-point equation has only the zero solution.
parts.hint_html: Compare the scale on the invariant line with 1.

marking_points.criterion_html: Justify that only the origin is fixed.

parts.label: e
